Config: config/params.base_case.yaml · Author's base case, 21 Nov 2026: assumptions, not findings · seed 42 · 1,000 runs
DEMO PARAMETERS: every limit, rate and probability in this report is made up. Nothing here is a finding.

What happens to a cohort of job-linked bridges under these settings, run 1,000 times. Use it to see which settings matter and by how much. It does not say what will happen: no Malaysian loss data exists, so every probability below is an input.

Developmental pricing

DEVELOPMENTAL PRICING: this product is priced below a commercial return on purpose. The funders accept a planned loss in return for additionality.

The DFI and the guarantor knowingly price at or below cost to reach borrowers the market does not serve. This section shows that planned loss, counting everything the DFI and the guarantor put in, the reserve included (they are the sponsors): it is the price, not a forecast. It assumes no additionality; whether the bridge reaches new-to-credit borrowers and unlocks jobs is measured in the pilot (gate 4), and the cost per additional borrower below is an illustration across shares, not a finding. The borrower's all-in charge is capped: financier fee + guarantee fee ≤ the cap, charged on the drawn amount, simple interest. No loss budget is set yet.

The guarantee fee is above the all-in cap, so nothing is left for the financier. Choose a lower guarantee fee or a higher cap.

Risk and return: the DFI and the guarantor

Each party carries its own costs. The DFI pays interest on the debt that funds the loans, holds equity against them, and bears the cost to serve. The guarantor sets its cap aside as capital for the length of a cohort and pays an admin cost per bridge. The costs are demo placeholders, empty in the real template: the DFI and the guarantor must supply their own. Return on capital is compared with each party's required return, and the gap is the spread it earns. Risk is shown as a bad group, the average of the worst 5% of groups, and the chance of a loss-making group. The DFI and the guarantor are the sponsors: they fund the first-loss reserve between them, so the last rows show each party after funding its share.

The guarantee fee is above the all-in cap here, so nothing is left for the DFI.

The reserve: funded by the DFI and the guarantor

There is no outside sponsor: the DFI and the guarantor are the sponsors. They fund the first-loss reserve between them, the guarantor 0% and the DFI 100% here (a placeholder split), up front, into a ring-fenced account (a promise is not enough: the guarantor's cover sits on top of it). Losses use it first. What the cohort does not spend goes back to the two of them once its loans are closed and recoveries are in. Each party is charged for its money tied up for 210 days (the cohort plus the write-off period) at its own required return. The other columns use the config's own cover, guarantee fee, all-in cap and cost to serve.

A bigger reserve is not free here: it is the same two parties' money. It moves the point where the guarantor starts paying further above the expected loss, but each party has to put up cash for it. The joint result is what the two of them lose or earn together, so it shows how much real money the programme costs them.

Path to viability

Can the product work at the all-in cap, and what would it take? A loan earns by time but loses by the loan: the cap earns only a few per cent of a short loan, while cash payments to the painter, damaged projects and a high cost to serve each cost more than that. Move the five levers and watch the verdict. The DFI and the guarantor are the only funders, so the joint result is the real money they lose or earn together. When a loan can work, the section shows the fee each party would need: the cap has to be split so that both earn their required return, and today's split may not be it. When a gap remains, it is priced per additional borrower, which is what to ask a party that values additionality to pay.

Assumptions: the chance of damage, lateness and cash payments per loan does not change with the tenor, and a longer tenor earns more because the cap is a rate a year. Both are placeholders until the pilot measures them.

Damage rate and the loss trip wire

A trip wire pauses new loans when the loss so far, after recoveries, passes a line, counted as a share of the money lent on loans whose outcome is already known. It trades reach for loss: every loan not made is a borrower not reached, which is what developmental pricing is paying for. It also cannot stop loans already out: outcomes arrive about 10 loans late here, and the wire cannot fire before 50 loans have a known outcome. Damage is the two endings abandoned and rejected; late payments and cash to the painter keep the chances in the config. Each setting is run on the same random draws as the no-trip-wire case, so the loss avoided and loans given up are paired, not noise.

Damage, late and cash chances add to more than 100% for this setting.

Method and limits

  • One run is one cohort. Each job draws a materials cost and a deposit; the bridge amount uses the same rule as the live release decision, and stops at the cohort cap.
  • Each bridge draws one outcome. Loss = amount × (1 − recovery rate for that outcome).
  • Losses run through the layers in event order: the reserve is shared across the cohort, then the guarantor up to its cap, then the financier.
  • The guarantee fee is charged to the borrower on drawn amounts and passed to the guarantor.
  • The stop line uses the bypass rate to date, tested once the minimum number of bridges is out.
  • Not modelled: changes in behaviour from pricing or margin of advance, correlation between bridges, collection costs beyond cost to serve, timing of cash.
Sensitivity tool, not a forecast. All parameters are pilot settings. Views are the author's own. Not financial advice.
